shelf_items.name: Suzanne de la Monte / Type 3 diabetes hypothesis
shelf_items.what_it_found: Alzheimer's involves brain insulin resistance and impaired insulin signaling, not amyloid accumulation. De la Monte showed that intranasal insulin improves cognition in early AD.
shelf_items.evidence_strength: Multiple small RCTs (e.g., Craft et al., 2012) showing cognitive improvement with intranasal insulin; replicated in animal models.
shelf_items.why_buried: Amyloid hypothesis dominated funding and research; insulin resistance was seen as a separate diabetes issue, not central to AD.
shelf_items.current_status: Being rediscovered; intranasal insulin trials ongoing, but still underfunded relative to amyloid.

shelf_items.name: Ruth Itzhaki / Herpes simplex virus (HSV-1) hypothesis
shelf_items.what_it_found: HSV-1 DNA found in AD brains; antiviral treatment (e.g., acyclovir) reduces AD risk in infected individuals. Itzhaki showed HSV-1 triggers amyloid deposition as a protective response.
shelf_items.evidence_strength: Epidemiological studies (e.g., Tzeng et al., 2018) show antiviral use reduces AD risk by 90%; replicated in cell and animal models.
shelf_items.why_buried: Infectious cause was dismissed as fringe; amyloid hypothesis focused on proteinopathy, not pathogens.
shelf_items.current_status: Gaining traction; clinical trials of antivirals (e.g., valacyclovir) underway, but still marginalized.

shelf_items.name: Jack de la Torre / Vascular hypothesis
shelf_items.what_it_found: AD is primarily a vascular disorder: reduced cerebral blood flow precedes cognitive decline. De la Torre proposed that restoring blood flow (e.g., via exercise, vasodilators) could prevent or reverse AD.
shelf_items.evidence_strength: Observational studies show low cerebral blood flow predicts AD; exercise interventions improve cognition in mild cognitive impairment (MCI).
shelf_items.why_buried: Amyloid hypothesis ignored vascular contributions; funding went to amyloid-clearing drugs.
shelf_items.current_status: Still buried; vascular risk factor management is recommended but not central to AD research.

shelf_items.name: George Perry / Oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction
shelf_items.what_it_found: AD brains show massive oxidative damage and mitochondrial dysfunction early in disease, before amyloid plaques appear. Perry argued amyloid is a compensatory response to oxidative stress.
shelf_items.evidence_strength: Extensive biochemical evidence; antioxidants (e.g., vitamin E) show modest benefit in some trials (e.g., Sano et al., 1997).
shelf_items.why_buried: Amyloid hypothesis overshadowed oxidative stress; antioxidant trials failed due to poor design or dosing.
shelf_items.current_status: Still buried; mitochondrial therapies (e.g., MitoQ) being tested but not mainstream.

shelf_items.name: Dale Bredesen / Multi-factorial approach (ReCODE protocol)
shelf_items.what_it_found: AD is driven by multiple factors (insulin resistance, inflammation, toxins, infections, nutrient deficiencies). Bredesen's protocol targeting these factors reversed cognitive decline in some patients.
shelf_items.evidence_strength: Case series and small trials (e.g., Bredesen et al., 2016) show cognitive improvement; not yet replicated in large RCTs.
shelf_items.why_buried: Amyloid hypothesis demanded a single-target drug; multi-factorial approach was seen as unscientific and hard to patent.
shelf_items.current_status: Being rediscovered; functional medicine practitioners use it, but mainstream remains skeptical.

shelf_items.name: William H. Frey II / Intranasal insulin and other peptides
shelf_items.what_it_found: Intranasal delivery of insulin and other peptides (e.g., GLP-1) improves memory in AD and MCI by bypassing the blood-brain barrier and targeting insulin receptors.
shelf_items.evidence_strength: Multiple small RCTs (e.g., Craft et al., 2012; Claxton et al., 2015) show cognitive improvement; replicated in animal models.
shelf_items.why_buried: Amyloid hypothesis dominated; intranasal insulin was seen as a diabetes drug, not an AD treatment.
shelf_items.current_status: Ongoing trials (e.g., SNIFF trial); still underfunded.

shelf_items.name: Mark Smith / Amyloid as a protective response
shelf_items.what_it_found: Amyloid beta is an antimicrobial peptide and antioxidant; it accumulates as a protective response to infection or oxidative stress, not as a primary cause.
shelf_items.evidence_strength: Biochemical and cell culture evidence; amyloid beta kills microbes in vitro.
shelf_items.why_buried: Directly contradicted the amyloid cascade hypothesis; Smith was marginalized and funding dried up.
shelf_items.current_status: Still buried; some researchers now acknowledge amyloid's protective role, but no major shift.
